item.title: Former Federal Prosecutor to Investigate Cornell Sexual Assault Claims
item.description:
The New York attorney general on Wednesday appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor in Manhattan, to lead a criminal investigation into a former Cornell University student’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity party in 2024.

Ms. Kelly served as the inaugural chief of the civil rights unit in the criminal division of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York.

In the Cornell investigation, she will oversee a team of lawyers both from the attorney general’s office and from the firm Boies Schiller Flexner, where Ms. Kelly is now a partner, according to a news release.

The team will review evidence and interview witnesses related to what the former Cornell student, now known as Jane Doe, described in a lawsuit as a sexual encounter that began on Oct. 19, 2024, and spiraled into a drug-fueled assault inside a fraternity house by several men.

All of the men have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.

“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Ms. Kelly said. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the office of the attorney general as we examine all available evidence.”

In a news release, the attorney general, Letitia James, said she is confident that Ms. Kelly will lead a “fair and comprehensive investigation.”

The appointment of Ms. Kelly follows a weekslong search by the attorney general for a lawyer who would take on a case that has convulsed Cornell’s campus in Ithaca, N.Y., and plunged the Ivy League institution into crisis.

In making the appointment, Ms. James has selected a veteran litigator who has overseen high-profile sex crimes prosecutions, including by leading the team that won the conviction of the hip-hop mogul Sean Combs of prostitution-related offenses last year. Mr. Combs was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking, the most serious charges against him.

But Ms. James has also enlisted the aid of a firm with a complicated history of involvement in other such cases.

Lawyers from Boies Schiller Flexner have represented victims of the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And one of its founding partners, David Boies, was also close to the disgraced Hollywood film producer Harvey Weinstein. Mr. Weinstein was accused in 2017 by multiple women of abusing his power to sexually assault them, and he was later convicted of sex crimes in New York and California.

Before articles appeared in The New York Times detailing some of the allegations against Mr. Weinstein, Mr. Boies personally signed a contract with a private intelligence firm that was hired to quash the articles about Mr. Weinstein.

A representative of Boies Schiller Flexner did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Kelly did not join the firm until July 2025.

In the Cornell case, the former student’s allegations were detailed in a lawsuit filed in Manhattan on Sept. 16. The suit unleashed a flood of outrage on social media and college campuses over the handling of her claims, both by the university and the Tompkins County district attorney, Matthew Van Houten.

Ms. Kelly’s appointment also comes amid criticism of Ms. James, who has been accused of showing bias in describing the case on social media.

On Sept. 28, the same day that Mr. Van Houten issued a statement saying he would reopen a criminal inquiry into the former student’s allegations, Ms. James posted on social media that what Jane Doe “has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.”

“I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers,” Ms. James wrote at the time. “To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”

Later that week, Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had “lost faith” in Mr. Van Houten, who had initially declined to pursue a criminal case in response to Jane Does’s earlier complaint. In the same statement, Ms. Hochul said she had appointed Ms. James as special prosecutor to oversee a new investigation into the case.

After Ms. James was appointed, her office said it had narrowed the search for outside counsel to support the investigation.

But in two separate filings in the weeks since, lawyers for men accused by Jane Doe have argued that Ms. James should be removed from the investigation and that a separate special prosecutor should be appointed. A hearing in one of those matters was held in Sullivan County Supreme Court last week, where lawyers for Ms. James defended her against one of the motions. A judge has yet to make a ruling on the request to remove Ms. James.

Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer representing the man whose request was heard in Sullivan County, said Ms. Kelly’s appointment “changes the face of the investigation without establishing any change in ultimate authority.”

“Nothing announced today states that Attorney General James has recused herself, relinquished supervisory or charging authority, or surrendered the ability to direct, approve, reject, or override substantive prosecutorial decisions,” he said.

Ms. Kelly’s appointment would offer Ms. James’s office, which does not typically prosecute sex crimes, added experience to the Cornell investigation.

After getting a bachelor's degree from Cornell and a law degree from Columbia University, Ms. Kelly began her legal career at an international law firm. She then clerked for federal judges in Manhattan and New Jersey.

During her time as a federal prosecutor, Ms. Kelly oversaw cases spanning from fraud and racketeering to human trafficking.

item.title: The Blue Tsunami
item.description:
Good morning. Democrats flipped the House and the Senate, and they won key races for governor. The blue wave became a red wipeout, my colleague Lisa Lerer writes.

Young people swung left in the election. In Austin, Texas, honks, singing, cheers and chants filled the streets, and college students gathered to celebrate shocking upsets: James Talarico, a progressive seminarian, won his Senate seat, and Gina Hinojosa won her race for governor. And in Michigan, students gathered to support Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat who won his Senate race.

And some Gen Z candidates won their races. We have more on that below.

Here’s what went down:

The top takeaways from the midterms.

1. The midterms showed that voters are angry at President Trump, who appears to have lost the coalition that elected him to the White House twice. Read more.

2. Trump said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the election results. He also said that he was prepared to work with Democrats and that Republicans lost because he was not on the ballot.

3. Turnout was high. In some places, turnout looked more like that of a presidential election. About 10 million votes were most likely cast in Texas, a record for a midterm election there. Young people shifted to the left by 32 points, according to our data.

4. Gerrymandering didn’t work. Republicans redrew maps in seven states, hoping for an edge. They didn’t get it.

5. Money couldn’t save conservatives. Republicans outspent Democrats, and hundreds of millions of dollars flooded the political system. The huge spending advantage didn’t matter.

6. The wins could mint a new generation of Democratic stars. Meet them.

Democrats flipped seven seats:

Texas: Talarico beat Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general. “We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love,” he said in his victory speech.

Michigan: El-Sayed will become the country’s first Muslim senator.

South Carolina: A Democrat and pediatrician, Annie Andrews, defeated Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, who had been appointed to fill her late brother Lindsey Graham’s seat.

Kansas: A megachurch pastor, Adam Hamilton, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since the Great Depression.

Maine: Senator Susan Collins lost her seat to Troy Jackson, a former Democratic state legislator.

Iowa: A Democratic state lawmaker and Paralympian, Josh Turek, flipped the state’s open Senate seat.

Ohio: A former Democratic senator, Sherrod Brown, won his seat back two years after he was ousted.

Florida: Senator Ashley Moody, a Republican, fended off a stronger-than-expected challenge from a democratic socialist to keep her seat, which was once held by Marco Rubio.

Results were still being counted in Alaska and Mississippi. It could be a while for Alaska.

Democrats have won 228 seats so far, and Republicans have lost most of the competitive races.

Texas: A moderate and Tejano music star, Bobby Pulido, flipped a House seat for Democrats.

Iowa: A Lutheran minister, Sarah Trone Garriott, flipped a key seat for Democrats. She beat a two-term incumbent who had aligned himself with Trump.

New York: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was re-elected to a fifth term. And Representative Mike Lawler, a Republican, conceded to his Democratic challenger, Cait Conley. (The Times has yet to call the race.)

Florida: A former high school teacher, Pia Dandiya, won an open seat in a district that Republicans had gerrymandered in their favor.

Texas: Hinojosa, a Democrat, defeated the three-term Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina elected to lead the state. It was a tectonic upset.

Georgia: Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history.

Ohio: In a bitter race, Amy Acton, a Democrat, defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican, after an ad he ran featuring her mother outraged members of both parties.

Read more takeaways, and follow our live coverage.

More than 100 Gen Z candidates filed to run for public office this election cycle.

How did they do overall?

Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Democrat, won the House seat in Colorado’s First District. She’ll become the first Gen Z woman in Congress. (Read more about Kiros.)

David Morales, a 28-year-old Democrat, will become the mayor of Providence, R.I.

Courtney McClain, a 25-year-old Democrat, lost the election for the House seat in South Carolina’s Fourth District but received about 45 percent of the vote.

Miami is at the top of the College Football Playoff rankings, followed by Georgia, Utah and Indiana. See the full list.

Some of the largest donations to universities are coming from donors without traditional ties to them.

A federal judge dismissed Trump’s lawsuit that sought to force Harvard to turn over its admissions documents in connection with a government discrimination investigation.

Pilates bros are here. The exercise has long been seen as a women’s workout, but some guys — including Tom Brady, LeBron James, Cristiano Ronaldo and me — have been trying it out. The shaking after a Pilates class is literally unreal.

Is it rude to ask a friend to stay with you? Someone on TikTok posted a video criticizing couch-surfers, and it set off a debate about what friends owe each other.

Do this to get ahead.

Start your holiday shopping early. Our 2026 Holiday Gift Guide has dropped, and there are so many options to choose from. I need to start adding things to my list!

Go for a scenic walk. Our writer walked across several bridges on the Hudson River and came away with a new perspective.

How well do you know your book adaptations? These novels about animals were made into popular movies. Take our quiz.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com

Lauren Jackson edited Extra Credit today. Eli Cohen and Marika Kochiashvili were our photo editors.
